## Two views of one output distribution

- So far: a generative model = a fitted distribution you can sample
- Now two deeper views of the *same output distribution*, each one line long:
- **View 1 — hierarchy:** sample step by step, conditionally (a hierarchical
  latent-variable model)
- **View 2 — a map:** a deterministic function of *all* the base randomness

[Every generative sampler — diffusion included — is View 2, once all of its random inputs are exposed.]{.big}

## View 1: conditional generation

$$\mathbb{P}(z = 1) = \pi, \quad \mathbb{P}(z = 2) = 1-\pi,
\qquad x \mid z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma^2)$$

- Draw the hidden label $z$ (the **latent variable**), then draw from the chosen Gaussian
- This is **ancestral sampling**: follow the arrows of the hierarchy
- The marginal you observe is the two-component mixture:
  $p(x) = \pi\,\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma^2) + (1-\pi)\,\mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\sigma^2)$

::: {.note}
Generation runs $z \to x$. Inference runs $x \to z$: the posterior
$\mathbb{P}(z \mid x)$. For $\mu = \pm 1$ and $\pi = \tfrac12$, the posterior mean
of $\mu_z$ was W01's tanh denoiser — you have already met conditional inference.
:::

## View 2: marginalize the coin away

The **inverse-CDF construction**: for any CDF $F$, with the generalized inverse
$F^{-1}(u) = \inf\{x : F(x) \ge u\}$,

$$u \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = F^{-1}(u) \ \text{ has CDF } F$$

- Proof (continuous, strictly increasing case) is one line:
  $\mathbb{P}(F^{-1}(U) \le x) = \mathbb{P}(U \le F(x)) = F(x)$
- All the randomness lives in one uniform number; everything after it is **deterministic**
- Careful: $u < \pi$ selects the lowest $\pi$-fraction of the *mixture* — when the
  components overlap, that is **not** the original label $z$ (the packed map in the
  notes is the version that does encode the coin)

## The two-point limit

Slide $\sigma \to 0$ in the demo. The CDF becomes a staircase: jump at $\mu_1$,
plateau at height $\pi$, jump at $\mu_2$. The map becomes

$$x = \operatorname{sign}(u - \pi) \qquad \text{(for } \mu = \pm 1\text{; almost surely — } u = \pi \text{ has probability zero)}$$

- W01's two-point dataset, generated by **thresholding a uniform** — and in this
  separated limit, $u < \pi$ *does* coincide with the label
- Pure sampling has become a formula (Part 3 proves this limit)
- The plateau of $F$ is the empty region between the clusters: no $u$ ever lands there

## Why this reframing matters

| Model | Random input(s) | Sampling mechanism | Typical fitting |
|---|---|---|---|
| This demo | $u \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$ | quantile $F^{-1}(u)$ (numerical here) | the CDF is known |
| GAN | $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$ | $G_\theta(z)$, a network | adversarial objective |
| VAE | $z$, plus decoder noise $\varepsilon$ | sample $p_\theta(x \mid z)$, i.e. $T_\theta(z,\varepsilon)$ | ELBO / variational learning |
| Normalizing flow | $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$ | invertible $f_\theta(z)$ | exact likelihood (change of variables) |
| **Diffusion** | $x_T \sim \mathcal{N}$; step noise if stochastic | **probability-flow ODE** (deterministic) or reverse SDE | **score/denoising objectives, ELBO** |

Same outer skeleton: simple randomness → sampling mechanism → data. The learned
object, the constraints, and the sampler differ.

## You have already seen the diffusion map

- W01, Act III: particles from a moment-matched Gaussian flowed *numerically* to
  within $\approx \sigma_{\min}$ of $\pm 1$ (Euler steps, finite cloud — W01 lists
  the approximations)
- With the exact terminal law, exact score, and exact integration, the
  **probability-flow ODE is a deterministic transport** — an inverse-CDF-like map
  from noise to data
- Diffusion learns the **scores** of the noised distributions; integrating the
  resulting velocity field *constructs* the endpoint map

::: {.note}
When no formula for the map exists, we learn an ingredient of it. Learning that
ingredient — carefully, with all the mathematics — is the rest of this course.
:::

## {.accent}

::: {.quote}
Once every random draw is exposed, generation is a deterministic map from base
randomness to a sample.
